I'm confused about UPCs and ISRCs. Do I need both for my album, and what's the difference? [Context: {}]

You absolutely need both a UPC (Universal Product Code) and ISRCs (International Standard Recording Codes) for your album, as they serve distinct but equally critical functions in the music industry. The UPC identifies the entire product – in your case, the album itself. Think of it as the barcode for the entire collection of songs, enabling digital retailers to track its sales as a single unit. Each album, EP, or single release will have one unique UPC.

ISRCs, on the other hand, identify each individual track (sound recording) on your album. Every single song on your album, including bonus tracks or alternate versions, must have its own unique ISRC. This allows for precise tracking of plays, downloads, and royalties for that specific recording, regardless of which album or compilation it appears on. So, for an album with 10 tracks, you'd need one UPC for the album and 10 separate ISRCs, one for each song.

Here at indii, our system streamlines the assignment of both UPCs and ISRCs during the release creation process. We'll ensure your album receives a unique UPC and that each track gets its own valid ISRC, adhering to global standards. This precise identification is crucial for accurate royalty collection and content management across all DSPs. How do I get an ISRC for my new track, and what format should it be in for Spotify? [Context: {}]

Getting an ISRC (International Standard Recording Code) for your track is a fundamental step, as it uniquely identifies your sound recording worldwide for sales and royalty tracking. Here at indii, we make this process straightforward. When you're setting up a new single or album release within the indii platform, our system will automatically assign a new ISRC for each track if you don't already have one. This ensures compliance and proper tracking across all DSPs. The format is typically a 12-character alphanumeric code, like 'US-XYZ-23-00001', which includes country code, registrant code, year of reference, and a designation code.

For major DSPs like Spotify, Apple Music, and Amazon, the ISRC format generated by indii is fully compliant with industry standards. While the ISRC itself isn't directly visible to the listener on Spotify, it's crucial metadata used internally by the platform for content ID, royalty payouts, and rights management. It's essential that this code is accurate and unique to your specific sound recording. If you're porting an existing track from another distributor, you should always use the original ISRC to maintain its historical data.

When you're preparing your release, make sure to input all required metadata accurately alongside your audio files. Our platform performs real-time validation to catch any potential errors before submission. If you have any deeper questions about intellectual property or specific licensing requirements tied to your ISRC, the <<<SYSTEM_ORCHESTRATION>>> rights_management specialist is available to provide detailed guidance and ensure your IP is fully protected and properly monetized.

I want my new single to drop next Friday. Is that enough time to get it on all major platforms like Apple Music and Amazon? [Context: {}]

While it's technically possible to submit a release with a very short lead time, aiming for 'next Friday' is typically not recommended for a smooth and successful rollout, especially if you want it live on all major DSPs like Apple Music, Spotify, and Amazon exactly on that date. (Mode A) Standard industry best practice, and what we advise at indii, is to schedule your release with a minimum lead time of 2-4 weeks, or even longer (4-6 weeks) if you plan extensive marketing activities like pre-saves or pitching to editorial playlists.

(Mode B) This lead time allows for several crucial steps: our internal QC process, the ingestion and processing time required by each individual DSP (which can vary significantly), and crucially, time for pre-save links to generate and for you to execute your pre-release marketing campaign. Submitting too close to your desired release date risks delays, meaning your track might not appear on all platforms simultaneously, or even worse, could miss your target release date entirely. Our indii release scheduler will guide you on appropriate lead times.

(Mode C) We understand the excitement of releasing new music, but a well-planned release schedule is vital for maximizing your impact. It ensures your music is available everywhere on time and gives you the runway for effective promotion. For strategic advice on how to best leverage pre-saves, marketing campaigns, and playlist pitching around your release date, the <<<SYSTEM_ORCHESTRATION>>> marketing specialist is your go-to resource. They can help you craft a plan that aligns with the lead times required for distribution.

I'm moving my entire back catalog of 10 albums from my old distributor to indii. How can I do this without my songs disappearing from DSPs for a while? [Context: {}]

Migrating an entire back catalog can seem daunting, but it's a routine process we handle at indii, and we've developed a 'painless migration' strategy specifically to avoid gaps in availability on DSPs. (Mode A) The key is to ensure continuous presence. You should *never* issue a takedown request to your old distributor before your catalog is fully ingested and live with indii. Doing so will inevitably lead to your music disappearing from DSPs, which can negatively impact your streaming numbers, playlist placements, and listener access.

(Mode B) Here's the indii process: First, you'll upload your entire catalog to indii, including all audio files and *all original metadata*, critically ensuring you use the *exact same ISRCs and UPCs* that were assigned by your previous distributor. Our system is designed to recognize and validate these existing identifiers. Once your catalog is fully processed by indii and appears live on all major DSPs (this can take 2-4 weeks), *then* and only then, you should initiate a takedown request with your old distributor. Because the ISRCs and UPCs remain consistent, DSPs will simply switch the content provider, maintaining your stream counts and availability.

(Mode C) This methodical approach guarantees a seamless transition, protecting your historical data and maintaining uninterrupted access for your fans. We understand how vital your back catalog is to your career, and our support team is here to guide you through each step. For any concerns about the portability of your ISRCs/UPCs or ensuring the legal continuity of your distribution rights during this migration, the <<<SYSTEM_ORCHESTRATION>>> rights_management specialist can provide expert assistance.
